We then manipulate two different types of parameters, the state means μ and the transition probabilities $A$, while keeping all remaining parameters the same between the groups. In the first case, we manipulate one state’s mean between the groups, that is:

$$
\theta^{1}=[\pi^{1},A^{1},\mu^{1},Σ^{1}]
$$



$$
\theta^{2}=[\pi^{1},A^{1},\mu^{2},Σ^{1}]
$$

where μ2 is obtained by simply adding a Gaussian noise vector to the state mean vector of one state:

$$
\mu_{1}^{2}=\mu_{1}^{1}+\phi
$$

Here, $\phi$ is the Gaussian noise vector of size 1 x $M$, $M$ is the number of parcels, here 50, and $\mu_{1}^{1}$ and $\mu_{1}^{2}$ are the first rows (corresponding to the first state) of the state mean matrices for groups 1 and 2, respectively. We control the amplitude of $\phi$ so that the difference between $\mu_{1}^{2}$ and $\mu_{1}^{1}$ is smaller than the minimum distance between any pair of states within one HMM. This is to ensure that the HMM recovers the difference between groups as difference in one state’s mean vector, rather than detecting a new state for group 2 that does not occur in group 1 and consequently collapsing two other states. Since the state means μ and the state covariances $Σ$ are the first- and second-order parameters of the same respective distributions, it is to be expected that, although we only directly manipulate μ, $Σ$ changes as well.

In the second case, we manipulate the transition probabilities for one state between the groups, while keeping all other parameters the same, i.e.:

$$
\theta^{1}=[\pi^{1},A^{1},\mu^{1},Σ^{1}]
$$



$$
\theta^{2}=[\pi^{1},A^{2},\mu^{1},Σ^{1}]
$$

where $A^{2}$ is obtained by randomly permuting the probabilities of one state to transition into any of the other states, excluding self-transition probability:

$$
A_{1,1}^{2}=A_{1,1}^{1}
$$



$$
A_{1,2:K}^{2}=pA_{1,2:K}^{1}
$$

Here, $p$ is a random permutation vector of size ($K$–1) x 1, $A_{1,1}^{1}$ and $A_{1,1}^{2}$ are the self-transition probabilities of state 1, and $A_{1,2:K}^{1}$ and $A_{1,2:K}^{2}$ are the probabilities of state 1 to transition into each of the other states.

We then concatenate the generated timeseries

$$
X=[X^{1},X^{2}]X\inR^{Mx(N∗T)}
$$

containing 100 subjects for group 1 and 100 subjects for group 2, with 1200 timepoints and 50 parcels per subject. Note that we do not introduce any differences between subjects within a group, so that the between-group difference in HMM parameters should be the most dominant distinction and easily recoverable by the classifiers. We then apply the pipelines described above, running a new group-level HMM and constructing the linear versions of the naïve kernel, the naïve normalised kernel, and the Fisher kernel on these synthetic time series. The second case of simulations, manipulating the transition probabilities, only introduces a difference in few ($K$ - 1) features and keeps the majority of the features the same between the groups, while the first case introduces a difference in a large number of features ($M$ features directly, by changing one state’s mean vector, and an additional M x M features indirectly, as this state’s covariance matrix will also be affected). To account for this difference, we additionally construct a version of the kernels for the second case of simulations that includes only 𝜋 and $A$, removing the state parameters μ and $Σ$.

Finally, we use a support vector machine (SVM) in combination with the different kernels to recover the group labels and measure the error produced by each kernel. We repeat the whole process (generating timeseries, constructing kernels, and running the SVM) 10 times, in each iteration randomising on three levels: generating new random noise/permutation vectors to simulate the timeseries, randomly initialising the HMM parameters when fitting the group-level HMM to the simulated timeseries, and randomly assigning subjects to 10 CV folds in the SVM.

#### Separating training and test set

We also simulate data to understand the sensitivity of the different kernels to separating training and test set before or after running the HMM. While separating training and test set is generally considered to be the gold standard to avoid leakage of information, this strategy may cause issues when the training and test set are very different from each other. In the simplest case, this would cause models to poorly generalise, which we aim to assess with the train-test split. However, in the case of the Fisher kernel, features are not independent but defined in reference to a group set of parameters. That means that, if we train the HMM only on the training set and then construct the Fisher kernel of a group of test subjects that are very different from the training set, this difference will be overrepresented in the kernel and likely overshadow other, more subtle differences between individuals.

Similar to the feature importance simulations, we generate time courses for two groups of subjects from two HMMs: timeseries $X^{train}$ for the training set and timeseries $X^{test}$ for the test set, from HMMs with parameters $\theta^{train}$ and $\theta^{test}$:

$$
X^{train}∼HMM(\theta^{train})
$$



$$
X^{test}∼HMM(\theta^{test})X^{train},X^{test}\inR^{Mx((\frac{N}{2})∗T)}
$$

We use the group-level HMM fit to real data as the basis for the simulations, so that $HMM(\theta^{train})=HMM(\theta^{0})$. For the test set, we then add different levels of noise to one of the state’s mean vector to simulate varying degrees of between-group difference:

$$
\theta^{train}=[\pi^{train},A^{train},\mu^{train},Σ^{train}]
$$



$$
\theta^{test}=[\pi^{train},A^{train},\mu^{test},Σ^{train}]
$$



$$
\mu^{test}=[\mu_{1}^{train}+bϵ\mu_{2}^{train}...\mu_{k}^{train}]
$$

where $ϵ$ is the 1 x $M$ Gaussian noise vector representing the heterogeneity between the training and the test set and $b$ is a scalar controlling the noise level.

We randomly generate a continuous target variable, $Y$, which the models will aim to predict. We will simulate a single state’s mean to be correlated with this target variable, but we will add varying degrees of noise, which will make it gradually more difficult to predict the target. We do this by adding a fraction of the target variable and the noise to a second state mean vector for each subject in the training and the test set:

$$
\theta^{s}=[\pi^{s},A^{s},\mu^{s},Σ^{s}]
$$



$$
\mu^{s}=[\mu_{1}\mu_{2}+\frac{Y^{s}}{10}+c\phi^{s}...\mu_{k}]
$$

where $\mu_{k}$ is the 1 x $M$ state mean vector for state $k$, $Y^{s}$ is the simulated target variable and $\phi^{s}$ is the 1 x $M$ Gaussian noise vector, controlled by the scaler $c$. That means that the two effects (the target variable and the difference between training and test set) are represented in two separate states’ parameters. The models should be able to retrieve the variable of interest in one state while ignoring the between-group noise affecting another state.

We then simulate individual subjects’ timeseries for 50 training subjects and 50 test subjects, varying the values for $b$ (controlling the level of between-group difference) in the range $b=[0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9]$ and $c$ (controlling the level of noise on the target variable $Y$) in the range $c=[0.5,0.7,0.9,1.1,1.3,1.5,1.7,1.9]$. We then use two different training schemes: the first one where we train the HMM on all subjects (training and test set) before constructing the features (training: together) and the second one where we train the HMM only on the training subjects (training: separate). For the Fisher kernel, that means that the features for the subjects in the test set will be computed in reference to a group-level HMM which they are either part of (training: together) or not a part of (training: separate). We then use the same pipeline described above to predict the simulated target variables from the linear naïve kernel, the linear naïve normalised kernel, and the linear Fisher kernel.

Summary:

In this work, the authors use a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) to describe dynamic connectivity and amplitude patterns in fMRI data, and propose to integrate these features with the Fisher kernel to improve the prediction of individual traits. The HMM-Fisher Kernel approach was shown to achieve higher prediction accuracy with lower variance on many individual traits compared to alternate kernels and measures of static connectivity. claims.claim: A data-driven functional parcellation with 50 parcels was estimated using multi-session spatial ICA on the temporally concatenated data from all subjects.
claims.source: The parcellation was estimated from the data using multi-session spatial ICA on the temporally concatenated data from all subjects. Note that this means that there is no strict divide between the subjects used for training and the subjects for testing the later predictive models, so that there is potential for leakage of information between training and test set. However, since this step does not concern the target variable, but only the preprocessing of the predictors, the effect can be expected to be minimal (Rosenblatt et al., 2024). Using this approach, a data-driven functional parcellation with 50 parcels was estimated, where all voxels are weighted according to their activity in each parcel, resulting in a weighted, overlapping parcellation.
claims.evidence: This describes the parcellation method used, with citation about data leakage effects.

claims.source: We normalised the timecourses of each subject to ensure that the model of brain dynamics and, crucially, the kernels were not driven by (averaged) amplitude and variance differences between subjects.
claims.evidence: This describes a preprocessing step and its rationale.

claims.claim: The Hidden Markov model (HMM) is a generative probabilistic model, which assumes that an observed time-series was generated by a sequence of 'hidden states'.
claims.source: The Hidden Markov model (HMM) is a generative probabilistic model, which assumes that an observed time-series, such as BOLD signal in a given parcellation, was generated by a sequence of 'hidden states' (Baum and Eagon, 1967; Baum and Petrie, 1966).
claims.evidence: This describes the HMM, supported by citations.

claims.claim: In this study, HMM states are modeled as multivariate Gaussian distributions, defined both in terms of mean and covariance, which can be interpreted as distinct patterns of amplitude and FC.
claims.source: We here model the states as multivariate Gaussian distributions, defined both in terms of mean and covariance —which can be interpreted as distinct patterns of amplitude and FC (Vidaurre et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This describes how states are modeled in this study, with citation.

claims.claim: The number of states can be understood as the level of detail or granularity with which we describe the spatiotemporal patterns in the data, akin to a dimensionality reduction.
claims.source: The number of states can be understood as the level of detail or granularity with which we describe the spatiotemporal patterns in the data, akin to a dimensionality reduction, where a small number of states will lead to a very general, coarse description and a large number of states will lead to a very detailed, fine-grained description.
claims.evidence: This explains the interpretation of the number of states parameter.

claims.claim: The Fisher kernel is built upon a projection on the Riemannian manifold, so predictions based on this kernel account for the mathematical structure of the HMM.
claims.source: The Fisher kernel, as described below, is built upon a projection on this manifold, so predictions based on this kernel account for the mathematical structure of the HMM.
claims.evidence: This explains how the Fisher kernel relates to the HMM structure.

claims.claim: Dual estimation refers to the process of fitting the previously estimated group-level model again to a single subject's timeseries, so that the parameters from the group-level model are adapted to fit the individual.
claims.source: Dual estimation refers to the process of fitting the previously estimated group-level model again to a single subject's timeseries, so that the parameters from the group-level model HMM0 are adapted to fit the individual.
claims.evidence: This defines the dual estimation procedure.

claims.claim: Kernels are a convenient approach to accommodate nonlinearity and to work with high-dimensional, complex features, such as parameters from a model of brain dynamics.
claims.source: Kernels (Shawe-Taylor and Cristianini, 2004) are a convenient approach to accommodate nonlinearity and to work with high-dimensional, complex features, such as parameters from a model of brain dynamics.
claims.evidence: This describes the utility of kernels, with citation.

claims.claim: While feature matrices can be very high dimensional, a kernel is represented by a (no. of subjects by no. of subjects) matrix.
claims.source: While feature matrices can be very high dimensional, a kernel is represented by a (no. of subjects by no. of subjects) matrix.
claims.evidence: This describes a property of kernel representations.

claims.claim: Kernels are computationally very efficient, since in most cases the number of subjects will be smaller than the number of features.
claims.source: This makes kernels computationally very efficient, since in most cases the number of subjects will be smaller than the number of features —which, in the case of HMMs, can be very large (potentially, in the order of millions).
claims.evidence: This explains the computational efficiency of kernels.

claims.claim: In the naïve kernel, the kernel does not take relationships between the parameters into account and the parameters are on different scales.
claims.source: The naïve kernel is based on a simple vectorisation of the subject-specific version of the HMM's parameters, each on their own scale. This means that the kernel does not take relationships between the parameters into account and the parameters are here on different scales.
claims.evidence: This describes a limitation of the naïve kernel.

claims.claim: The naïve kernel procedure can be thought of as computing Euclidean distances between two sets of HMM parameters, ignoring the actual geometry of the space of parameters.
claims.source: This procedure can be thought of as computing Euclidean distances between two sets of HMM parameters, ignoring the actual geometry of the space of parameters.
claims.evidence: This explains what the naïve kernel does geometrically.

claims.claim: In the naïve kernel, a change of 0.1 in the transition probabilities between two states would be treated the same as a change of 0.1 in one entry of the covariance matrix of a specific state, even though these are very different types of changes.
claims.source: In this way, the different parameters in the feature vector are difficult to compare, since for example a change of 0.1 in the transition probabilities between two states is not of the same magnitude as a change of 0.1 in one entry of the covariance matrix of a specific state. In the naïve kernel, these two very different types of changes would be treated indistinctly.
claims.evidence: This illustrates a problem with the naïve kernel approach.

claims.claim: The naïve normalised kernel does not respect the geometry of the space of parameters.
claims.source: This kernel does not respect the geometry of the space of parameters either.
claims.evidence: This describes a limitation of the naïve normalised kernel.

claims.claim: The Fisher kernel is specifically designed to preserve the structure of a generative probabilistic model.
claims.source: The Fisher kernel (Jaakkola et al., 1999; Jaakkola and Haussler, 1998) is specifically designed to preserve the structure of a generative probabilistic model (here, the HMM).
claims.evidence: This describes a key property of the Fisher kernel, with citations.

claims.claim: In the Fisher kernel, similarity between subjects is defined in reference to a group-level model of brain dynamics.
claims.source: Similarity between subjects is here defined in reference to a group-level model of brain dynamics.
claims.evidence: This describes how similarity is defined in the Fisher kernel.

claims.claim: In the Fisher kernel, two subjects are defined as similar if the group-level model would have to be changed in a similar direction for both, and dissimilar otherwise.
claims.source: The similarity between subjects can then be described based on this score, so that two subjects are defined as similar if the group-level model would have to be changed in a similar direction for both, and dissimilar otherwise.
claims.evidence: This explains how similarity is determined in the Fisher kernel.

claims.claim: The Fisher score is given by the gradient of the log-likelihood with respect to each model parameter.
claims.source: More precisely, the Fisher score is given by the gradient of the log-likelihood with respect to each model parameter
claims.evidence: This provides the mathematical definition of the Fisher score.

claims.claim: In the linear Fisher kernel, the gradients of typical examples (i.e. subjects whose timeseries can be described by similar parameters as the group-level model) are close to zero, while gradients of atypical examples can be very large.
claims.source: One issue when working with the linear Fisher kernel is that the gradients of typical examples (i.e. subjects whose timeseries can be described by similar parameters as the group-level model) are close to zero, while gradients of atypical examples (i.e. subjects who are very different from the group-level model) can be very large.
claims.evidence: This describes a potential issue with the linear Fisher kernel.

claims.claim: The study used kernel ridge regression (KRR) to predict demographic and behavioural variables from the different kernels.
claims.source: Similarly to Vidaurre et al., 2021, we use kernel ridge regression (KRR) to predict demographic and behavioural variables from the different kernels (other kernel-based prediction models or classifiers such as a support vector machine are also possible).
claims.evidence: This describes the prediction method used, with citation.

claims.claim: The study used k-fold nested cross-validation (CV) to select and evaluate the models, with 10 folds for both the outer loop and the inner loop.
claims.source: We used k-fold nested cross-validation (CV) to select and evaluate the models. We used 10 folds for both the outer loop (used to train and test the model) and the inner loop (used to select the optimal hyperparameters) such that 90% were used for training and 10% for testing.
claims.evidence: This describes the cross-validation strategy used.

claims.claim: The study accounted for family structure in the HCP dataset so that subjects from the same family were never split across folds.
claims.source: In both the outer and the inner loop, we accounted for family structure in the HCP dataset so that subjects from the same family were never split across folds (Winkler et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological consideration, with citation.

claims.claim: Within the CV, sex and head motion confounds were regressed out by estimating the regression coefficients for the confounds on the training set and applying them to the test set.
claims.source: Within the CV, we regressed out sex and head motion confounds, that is we estimated the regression coefficients for the confounds on the training set and applied them to the test set (Snoek et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This describes the confound regression procedure, with citation.

claims.claim: The nested 10-fold CV was repeated 100 times to obtain a distribution of model performance values for each variable.
claims.source: We repeated the nested 10-fold CV 100 times, so that different combinations of subjects were randomly assigned to the folds at each new CV iteration to obtain a distribution of model performance values for each variable.
claims.evidence: This describes the repeated CV procedure.

claims.claim: The 100 random repetitions of the 10 outer CV folds were generated once and then used for training and prediction of all methods, so that all methods were fit to the same partitions.
claims.source: We generated the 100 random repetitions of the 10 outer CV folds once, and then used them for training and prediction of all methods, so that all methods were fit to the same partitions.
claims.evidence: This describes how consistency was maintained across methods.

claims.claim: Reliability concerns two aspects: (i) that the model will never show excessively large errors for single subjects that could harm interpretation; and (ii) that the model's accuracy will be consistent across random variations of the training set.
claims.source: The second criterion, reliability, concerns two aspects: (i) that the model will never show excessively large errors for single subjects that could harm interpretation; and (ii) that the model's accuracy will be consistent across random variations of the training set —in this case by using different (random) iterations for the CV folds.
claims.evidence: This defines the reliability criterion used in the study.

claims.claim: The study normalised the maximum absolute error (MAXAE) by dividing it by the range of the respective variable to make results comparable across different traits.
claims.source: Since the traits we predict are on different scales, the MAXAE is difficult to interpret, for example a MAXAE of 10 would be considered small if the true range of the variable we are predicting was 1,000, while it would be considered large if the true range of the variable was 1. To make the results comparable across the different traits, we therefore normalise the MAXAE by dividing it by the range of the respective variable.
claims.evidence: This explains the rationale for normalizing MAXAE.

claims.claim: The study considered the risk of large errors (NMAXAE >10), very large errors (NMAXAE >100), and extreme errors (NMAXAE >1000) as the percentage of runs where the model's NMAXAE exceeds the given threshold.
claims.source: We here consider the risk of large errors (NMAXAE >10), very large errors (NMAXAE >100), and extreme errors (NMAXAE >1000) as the percentage of runs (across variables and CV iterations) where the model's NMAXAE exceeds the given threshold.
claims.evidence: This defines the error risk thresholds used.

claims.claim: The reliability criterion in terms of maximum errors is that the risk of large errors (NMAXAE >10) should be 0%.
claims.source: Our reliability criterion in terms of maximum errors is therefore that the risk of large errors (NMAXAE >10) should be 0%.
claims.evidence: This defines the reliability criterion for maximum errors.

claims.claim: Robustness was quantified as the standard deviation of the correlation between model-predicted and actual values over 100 iterations and 10 folds of CV.
claims.source: We evaluated the robustness by iterating nested 10-fold CV 100 times for each variable, randomising the subjects in the folds at each iteration, so that the models would encounter a different combination of subjects in the training and test sets each time they are run. Looking at this range of 1000 accuracies (10 folds * 100 repetitions) for each variable, we can assess whether the model's performance changes drastically depending on which combinations of subjects it encountered in the training phase, or whether the performance is the same regardless of the subjects encountered in the training phase. The former would be an example of a model that is susceptible to changes in training examples and the latter an example of a model that is robust. We here quantify robustness as the standard deviation (S.D.) of the prediction accuracy r across the 10 folds and 100 CV iterations of each variable, where a small mean S.D. over variables indicates higher robustness.
claims.evidence: This defines how robustness was quantified.

claims.claim: The study tested for significant differences in mean prediction accuracy between the methods using repeated k-fold cross-validation corrected t-tests.
claims.source: We test for significant differences in mean prediction accuracy between the methods using repeated k-fold cross-validation corrected t-tests (Bouckaert and Frank, 2004).
claims.evidence: This describes the statistical testing method used, with citation.

claims.claim: All p-values were corrected across multiple comparisons using Benjamini-Hochberg correction to control the false discovery rate (FDR).
claims.source: All p-values are corrected across multiple comparisons using Benjamini-Hochberg correction to control the false discovery rate (FDR).
claims.evidence: This describes the multiple comparison correction method used.

results.result: The HMM-Fisher kernel approach accurately and reliably predicts individual traits from brain dynamics by preserving the mathematical structure of the underlying Hidden Markov Model through a mathematically principled construction that leverages time-varying amplitude and functional connectivity information.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C8, C14, C20, C67-C68 collectively establish the core methodological contribution and its validation. The approach is described as mathematically principled (C6, C14), empirically validated as accurate and reliable in fMRI data (C7, C20, C67), and the mechanism by which it works is clearly articulated (C8, C68). The convergence of theoretical foundation, methodological description, and empirical validation provides strong support.

results.result: The linear Fisher kernel demonstrates higher prediction accuracy than most alternative methods, significantly outperforming the linear naïve kernel and Selected Edges method, though many comparisons with other methods were not statistically significant.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C37 and C69 provide detailed statistical comparisons showing the linear Fisher kernel's performance. While the kernel shows the highest average accuracy among time-varying methods (C28, C69), only two comparisons reach statistical significance (C29: vs. naïve kernel, p=0.031; C34: vs. Selected Edges, p=0.031). The lack of significance in most comparisons (C30, C32, C33, C35, C36) is acknowledged by the authors (C69), providing an honest assessment of the results.

results.result: The linear Fisher kernel demonstrates superior reliability compared to other methods, with 0% risk of large errors and the most robust performance across cross-validation iterations among time-varying methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C50 and C70 provide comprehensive reliability assessment. The 0% risk of large errors for the linear Fisher kernel (C44, C45) is a concrete, quantitative finding. Robustness comparisons show the linear Fisher kernel as most robust among time-varying methods (C48, C49), with significant advantages over time-averaged KL divergence and Selected Edges methods (C50). The Gaussian naïve normalised kernel's poor performance (C46: 1.229% risk of large errors) provides a clear contrast.

results.result: The Fisher kernel is most sensitive to differences in state parameters (amplitude and functional connectivity patterns) rather than transition probabilities, as demonstrated through both simulations and real data analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C62 and C78 provide converging evidence from simulations and real data. Simulations show perfect recovery of state mean differences (C51, C52) but poor recovery of transition probability differences (C53, C54), leading to the interpretation in C55. When state parameters are excluded, the Fisher kernel can recover transition differences (C56, C57). Real data analysis confirms state parameters drive predictions (C58, C59), with this effect not explained by parameter count differences (C60). The consistency across simulation and real data strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Training the HMM on all subjects versus only training subjects has no significant effect on prediction accuracy in the real dataset (N=1001), but simulations reveal that the Fisher kernel's performance degrades when training and test sets are highly different due to its reference-based feature definition.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 and C80 address train-test separation effects. Real data shows no significant effects (C63, C64), but simulations reveal a principled limitation: the Fisher kernel defines features relative to a group average (C65), causing performance degradation with increasing group differences when training separately (C66, C80). This is an honest assessment of a methodological consideration with practical implications for heterogeneous datasets.

results.result: Working in Riemannian space improves prediction accuracy for both time-varying (HMM-based) and time-averaged functional connectivity methods, indicating that respecting the geometry of parameter spaces is important for predictive modeling in neuroscience.
results.evaluation: Claims C37 and C71 establish a general principle supported by statistical evidence. The significant improvement for time-averaged methods using tangent space embedding (C37: Ridge regression in Riemannian space vs. Ridge regression, p=0.0313) parallels the improvement seen in HMM-based methods. This convergence across different feature types (C71) supports the broader principle about the importance of geometric considerations.

results.result: The Fisher kernel approach significantly outperforms methods that do not account for model structure and methods based on time-averaged functional connectivity that ignore brain dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C21 and C22 make broad statements about significant outperformance, but the detailed results (C29-C36) show that only 2 of many comparisons reached statistical significance. While the Fisher kernel shows numerically higher accuracy in most comparisons, the lack of statistical significance in most cases makes the claim of 'significant outperformance' overstated. The claims appear to be summary statements that don't fully align with the nuanced statistical results.

results.result: The Fisher kernel maintains superior performance when using less data per subject (single session) or when modeling only covariance-based states, though overall accuracies decrease with less data, indicating that more timepoints enable better individual characterization.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 and C75 demonstrate robustness of the main findings across different data configurations. The Fisher kernel's relative advantage persists in alternative analyses (C39, C41), while the overall accuracy decrease with less data (C40, C75) is a reasonable finding that more data improves characterization. These supplementary analyses strengthen confidence in the main results.

results.result: Gaussian versions of the kernels are more error-prone, less robust to training set changes, and computationally more expensive than linear versions, making them less practical despite potentially higher accuracy in some cases.
results.evaluation: Claims C76 and C77 summarize findings about Gaussian kernels supported by detailed results (e.g., C46 showing high error risk for Gaussian naïve normalised kernel). The computational expense claim (C77) is reasonable given the additional hyperparameter τ requiring cross-validation. This provides practical guidance for method selection.

results.result: Non-kernel-based Euclidean time-averaged FC models (Ridge regression and Selected Edges) make predictions in a restricted range close to variable means, leading to weak relationships but smaller errors.
results.evaluation: Claim C38 describes an observation about prediction behavior, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1 providing supporting evidence. This represents a methodological insight about how different approaches behave, explaining why correlation coefficients and error metrics can give different impressions of performance.

results.result: Among the behavioral variables tested, age was best predicted, followed by language-related cognitive items (PicVocab, ReadEng).
results.evaluation: Claim C42 reports a straightforward empirical finding about which variables were most predictable. This is a descriptive result supported by the data analysis, providing context about the differential predictability of various traits.

results.result: The study used resting-state fMRI data from 1001 subjects from the Human Connectome Project, with each subject having four scanning sessions (4800 timepoints total), and estimated group-level HMMs followed by subject-specific dual estimation.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25 and C92-C96 describe the dataset and basic methodological approach. These are straightforward descriptions of the data source, sample characteristics, and HMM estimation procedure, well-documented with appropriate citations (C92) and clear specification of data usage (C96).

results.result: A data-driven 50-parcel functional parcellation was estimated using multi-session spatial ICA, chosen because dynamic FC changes are better detected in this parcellation, and timecourses were normalized to prevent amplitude/variance differences from driving the model.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99 describe preprocessing choices with clear rationale. The parcellation choice is justified by citation (C98), and the normalization step (C99) has a clear methodological purpose. The acknowledgment of potential data leakage in C97 with citation to work showing minimal effects demonstrates methodological transparency.

results.result: The study used kernel ridge regression with nested 10-fold cross-validation repeated 100 times, accounting for family structure, regressing out confounds within CV, and using the same partitions across all methods for fair comparison.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C132 describe the prediction and validation framework with appropriate methodological rigor. Family structure consideration (C129), proper confound handling (C130), repeated CV for robustness assessment (C131), and consistent partitions across methods (C132) all represent sound methodological practices with appropriate citations.

results.result: The study defined reliability as encompassing both absence of excessive errors (0% risk of NMAXAE >10) and robustness to training set variations (low standard deviation across CV iterations), using appropriate statistical tests with multiple comparison correction.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C140 define the evaluation criteria and statistical approach. The two-component reliability definition (C134) is well-justified, the normalization of maximum errors (C135-C137) enables fair comparison across variables, robustness quantification (C138) is appropriate, and statistical testing (C139, C140) follows established methods with proper multiple comparison correction.

results.result: The naïve kernels ignore the Riemannian manifold structure by treating HMM parameters as Euclidean, failing to account for relationships between parameters and treating changes in different parameter types (e.g., transition probabilities vs. covariance entries) as equivalent despite their different scales and meanings.
results.evaluation: Claims C26, C27, and C111-C113, C115 describe the conceptual and mathematical limitations of naïve kernels. These are accurate characterizations of what these kernels do (or fail to do) geometrically, with C113 providing a concrete example illustrating the problem. This establishes the motivation for the Fisher kernel approach.

results.result: The Fisher kernel preserves the structure of the HMM by defining similarity between subjects based on Fisher scores (gradients of log-likelihood), where subjects are similar if the group-level model would need to change in similar directions to better fit their data.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C117, C119-C120 describe the Fisher kernel's mathematical foundation with appropriate citations (C116). The explanation of how similarity is defined (C117, C119) and the mathematical definition of Fisher score (C120) are accurate descriptions of this established method applied to HMMs.

results.result: Current approaches to predicting individual traits from brain signals typically use structural or time-averaged measures, missing the temporal dynamics of brain activity, partly because dynamic patterns require complex high-dimensional models that are difficult to use for prediction, and reliability is often not considered.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4, C10, and C19 establish the motivation and context for the study. These represent reasonable characterizations of the field's state, with C10 supported by multiple citations. The identification of gaps (C3, C4, C19) provides clear motivation for the proposed approach.

results.result: The method has broad potential applications: it can be applied to other neuroimaging modalities (MEG/EEG), other kernel-based classifiers, other probabilistic generative models, combined with other data types through stacking or Multi Kernel Learning, and may benefit clinical applications, though generalization to other datasets remains to be demonstrated.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C74 and C82-C87 describe potential applications and future directions. While the flexibility claims (C73, C74) are reasonable given the mathematical framework, and multimodal combination approaches (C84-C86) are supported by citations, these are largely speculative (C72, C74, C82, C87 are marked as SPECULATION). The limitation acknowledgment (C82) is appropriate, but the broad applicability claims require empirical validation.

results.result: The Fisher kernel can be modified to recognize changes in transition probabilities if these are of interest for specific research questions, as demonstrated in simulations.
results.evaluation: Claim C79 is directly supported by the simulation results in C56-C57, which show that excluding state parameters allows the Fisher kernel to recover transition probability differences. This demonstrates the method's flexibility for different research questions.

results.result: The study uses Hidden Markov Models as state-space models to capture recurring patterns of brain activity and functional connectivity, with HMM parameters lying on a Riemannian manifold, and employs dual estimation to obtain subject-specific parameters; kernels provide a computationally efficient way to work with these high-dimensional parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C11-C13, C15, and C100-C102, C105-C108, C110 provide background on HMMs and kernels. These are accurate descriptions of established methods (with appropriate citations: C12, C13, C100, C101, C107) and their properties (C15, C102, C105, C108, C110). The dual estimation procedure (C106) is clearly defined.

results.result: The study evaluates methods based on two criteria: prediction accuracy (high correlation between predicted and actual values) and reliability (no excessive errors and robustness to training set variations), with reliability being especially important for interpreting prediction errors in applications like brain age assessment.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C18 define the evaluation framework with clear rationale. The two criteria (C16, C17) are well-justified, and the importance of reliability (C18) is supported by citations to relevant work on brain age. This establishes a comprehensive evaluation approach beyond simple accuracy.

results.result: The HCP 1200 Young Adult dataset used in this study is a large sample from a healthy, young population.
results.evaluation: Claim C81 is a straightforward description of the dataset characteristics, acknowledged as a limitation in the context of generalization (C82). This is an accurate characterization of the HCP dataset.

results.result: Clinical neuroscience has focused mainly on static or structural information, leaving brain dynamics information untapped; reliable predictions are essential for clinical applications, but standard cross-validation does not resolve issues of extreme errors and large variation; the proposed approach addresses this by accounting for model structure and thoroughly assessing accuracy, errors, and robustness.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C91 provide clinical context and implications. The gap identification (C88) is reasonable, the reliability requirement for clinical use (C89) is supported by citations, the finding about cross-validation limitations (C90) is demonstrated in the study, and the summary of the contribution (C91) accurately reflects the work's scope.

results.result: In the linear Fisher kernel, gradients of typical subjects (similar to group-level model) are close to zero while gradients of atypical subjects can be very large, which may underestimate similarity between typical subjects.
results.evaluation: Claim C123 describes a known property of Fisher kernels that motivates the use of Gaussian versions. This is an accurate characterization of a potential issue with the linear Fisher kernel, providing context for why Gaussian kernels might be considered despite their other limitations.

results.result: The study proposes combining Hidden Markov Models (HMM) with the Fisher kernel to predict individual traits from dynamic brain connectivity patterns. The Fisher kernel is constructed in a mathematically principled manner that preserves the structure of the HMM by respecting the Riemannian manifold geometry of the parameters. The authors claim this HMM-Fisher kernel approach accurately and reliably predicts traits from brain dynamics in fMRI data.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers affirm the study's main contribution. The editor states 'the evidence supporting the authors' conclusions is compelling' and describes the work as 'important.' Two reviewers explicitly note that 'the authors addressed adequately all my comments' and 'I believe this work will be an interesting contribution to the literature,' indicating acceptance of the core methodological claims.

results.result: The linear Fisher kernel demonstrated higher prediction accuracy than methods that do not account for model structure (naïve kernels) and time-averaged functional connectivity methods. Specifically, it significantly outperformed the linear naïve kernel (p=0.031) and the Selected Edges method (p=0.031), though comparisons with some other methods were not statistically significant.
results.evaluation: The reviewers accept these comparative findings without challenge. The editor notes the study includes 'comparing brain-behaviour prediction accuracies across a range of different traits, including out of sample assessment,' and one reviewer summarizes that 'the HMM-Fisher Kernel approach was shown to achieve higher prediction accuracy...compared to alternate kernels and measures of static connectivity,' indicating acceptance of the accuracy comparisons.

results.result: The linear Fisher kernel demonstrated superior reliability compared to other methods, with 0% risk of large errors (normalized maximum absolute error >10) and robust performance across different training set compositions. It was significantly more robust than time-averaged KL divergence (p=0.003) and Selected Edges (p<0.0001) methods.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the reliability findings without objection. One reviewer specifically notes the approach 'was shown to achieve higher prediction accuracy with lower variance on many individual traits,' directly acknowledging the reliability claims. The editor's statement that evidence is 'compelling' encompasses these reliability assessments.

results.result: Using tangent space embedding (Riemannian geometry) improved prediction accuracy for both time-varying HMM parameters and time-averaged covariance matrices. For time-averaged methods, Ridge regression in Riemannian space significantly outperformed standard Ridge regression (p=0.0313), indicating that respecting the geometric structure of predictors is important for neuroimaging prediction models.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this finding. The acceptance of the overall methodological framework and the lack of specific critique of the Riemannian geometry comparisons indicates implicit support. The editor's characterization of evidence as 'compelling' and reviewers' statements that comments were 'adequately addressed' suggest acceptance of these geometric considerations.

results.result: Simulation studies revealed that the Fisher kernel perfectly recovered group differences in state mean amplitude (0% error) and significantly outperformed other kernels (p<0.001). However, when differences were in transition probabilities, the Fisher kernel performed significantly worse than other kernels (p<0.01). When state parameters were excluded, the Fisher kernel could recover transition probability differences, indicating it is most sensitive to state parameters rather than transition dynamics.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these simulation findings without critique. One reviewer explicitly notes 'the authors demonstrate that parameters of the HMM state matrix may be more informative in predicting behavioral/cognitive variables in this data compared to state-transition probabilities,' directly acknowledging this result. The lack of any reviewer concern about these simulations indicates acceptance.

results.result: In real fMRI data, state parameters (amplitude and functional connectivity patterns) were the most relevant features for Fisher kernel predictions across all behavioral traits. Removing state features significantly diminished prediction accuracy (p=0.016), while removing transition features had no significant effect (p=0.480). This pattern held across all individual variables tested.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this feature importance analysis. One reviewer's summary that 'parameters of the HMM state matrix may be more informative' directly references this finding. The absence of any reviewer questioning of the feature ablation analysis and the overall positive assessment indicate acceptance of these claims about which HMM features drive predictions.

results.result: At the sample size used (N=1001), whether the HMM was trained on all subjects together versus only training subjects had no significant effect on prediction accuracy for any kernel. However, simulations showed that when training and test groups differ substantially, the Fisher kernel's performance can worsen when trained only on the training set, potentially leading to biased kernels that overestimate test subject dissimilarity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these train-test separation findings. The acceptance is implicit in the overall positive assessment and lack of specific critique. The editor's statement about 'out of sample assessment' being part of the compelling evidence suggests acceptance of the cross-validation approach and these findings about training schemes.

results.result: When using only one resting-state session (1200 timepoints) instead of all four sessions (4800 timepoints), the linear Fisher kernel still outperformed other HMM-based kernels, but overall accuracies were lower across all methods. This indicates that prediction of individual traits benefits from larger amounts of data per subject.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about this supplementary analysis. The implicit acceptance through overall positive assessment and lack of specific critique indicates these findings about data quantity requirements are accepted. This is treated as a supporting rather than central finding.

results.result: When HMM states were defined only in terms of covariance (functional connectivity) without mean amplitude, the Fisher kernel still outperformed other kernels at comparable accuracy levels.
results.evaluation: This supplementary analysis is not specifically discussed by reviewers but is accepted implicitly through the overall positive assessment. The lack of critique and the general acceptance of the methodological framework indicate support for this robustness check.

results.result: Gaussian versions of the kernels were generally more error-prone and susceptible to changes in training sets compared to linear versions, although they occasionally predicted more accurately in certain runs. Additionally, Gaussian kernels are computationally more expensive, making them less practical.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these findings about Gaussian versus linear kernels. The acceptance is implicit in the overall positive assessment. This is treated as a methodological detail rather than a central contribution, but the lack of reviewer concern indicates acceptance.

results.result: Among the behavioral variables tested, age was best predicted, followed by language-related cognitive items (PicVocab and ReadEng, both age-adjusted and unadjusted versions).
